items.explanation: A single horizontal stroke for one. It is read イチ when counting and in words like 一月 (いちがつ, January); the native reading appears in ひとつ (one thing).
items.culture_note: In legal documents and contracts, the formal character 壱 is used instead, because a single stroke could easily be changed into 二 or 三.

items.explanation: Two horizontal strokes, the lower one longer. It is read ニ when counting and in 二月 (にがつ, February); the native reading appears in ふたつ (two things).
items.mnemonic: Two fingers held sideways, one on top of the other.

items.explanation: Three horizontal strokes, the bottom one longest. It is read サン when counting and in 三月 (さんがつ, March); the native reading appears in みっつ (three things).
items.mnemonic: Three fingers held sideways: one more line than 二.

items.explanation: 四 has two readings for four: シ, as in 四月 (しがつ, April), and よん. Because シ sounds like 死 (death), people usually say よん when counting.
items.mnemonic: A box with four corners and two legs inside it.
items.culture_note: Four is considered unlucky because of that sound, so some hospitals and hotels in Japan skip room number 4.

items.explanation: It is read ゴ when counting and in 五月 (ごがつ, May); the native reading appears in いつつ (five things).
items.mnemonic: A capital I with an extra hook tucked inside its belly.

items.explanation: It is read ロク when counting and in 六月 (ろくがつ, June); the native reading appears in むっつ (six things).
items.mnemonic: A little stick figure with a hat and two legs, standing on six toes.

items.explanation: 七 is read シチ, as in 七月 (しちがつ, July), or なな. When counting, people often say なな because しち and いち are easy to mix up.
items.mnemonic: A 7 turned upside down and crossed out.

items.explanation: Two strokes that spread apart. It is read ハチ when counting and in 八月 (はちがつ, August); the native reading appears in やっつ (eight things).
items.mnemonic: Two lines opening out like a fan.
items.culture_note: Eight is considered a lucky number because the shape widens toward the bottom, suggesting prosperity that keeps growing.

items.explanation: 九 is read キュウ or ク. The month is 九月 (くがつ, September), but when counting people usually say きゅう, because く sounds like 苦 (suffering).
items.mnemonic: An arm bent at the elbow, reaching for the last number before ten.

items.explanation: A cross for ten. Bigger numbers are built from it: 十一 (じゅういち) is ten plus one, 二十 (にじゅう) is two tens. The native reading appears in とお (ten things).
items.mnemonic: A plus sign: add up all ten fingers.
